To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in pregnant women, rising temperature in the 21–35 days prior to glucose tolerance screening was associated with beta cell impairment and an increased risk for GDM.
in pregnant women, rising ambient temperature in the 4 weeks prior (but not the week of) antepartum glucose tolerance testing may increase the risk of gestation diabetes mellitus.

in pregnant women undergoing antepatrum screening for gestational diabetes mellitus (GDM), daily changes in temperature in February – July (when mean daily temperatures are rising) are associated with poorer beta cell function, higher blood glucose, and an increased risk for GDM.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of environmental temperature on the physiology of glucose metabolism in pregnant women and the risk of GDM.
the effects of temperature changes on glucose tolerance.
the relationship between temperature and blood glucose in pregnancy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the impact of temperature on GDM risk is complex and may be mediated via multiple pathways.
rising temperature in the 2–4 weeks preceding the OGTT is associated with poorer beta cell function, which may contribute to a greater risk of GDM in the subsequent weeks.
in pregnant women, rising ambient temperature in the weeks prior to antepartum glucose tolerance testing is associated with beta cell failure, hyperglycaemia and an increased risk for GDM.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
temperature change is a better predictor of GDM than mean temperature.
the risk of GDM increases with the degree of temperature change in the weeks prior to glucose testing, and that this effect is most pronounced in months where mean temperature is rising.
rising environmental temperature in early to mid-pregnancy, in the 3 to 4 weeks prior, may be associated with an increased risk of gestational hyperglycaemia and gestational diabetes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in order to reduce the burden of GDM, the effects of temperature on beta cell dysfunction and glucose metabolism in pregnancy should be considered.
, in February – August, the risk of GDM may be reduced by maintaining a relatively constant temperature.
the impact of temperature on beta cell dysfunction and glucose tolerance may be delayed, with the effects of a given day of exposure persisting for several days thereafter.
